The amendments are not marked in the copy of the bill that I have, but section 3 is printed as amended, and reads as follows:
(1 )[DOT] The war veterans' allowance committee shall consist of three members to be appointed by the governor in council, one of whom shall be appointed chairman and shall receive a salary of six thousand dollars a year and the other two of whom shall receive each a salary of five thousand dollars a year; provided that the governor in council may appoint, to be additional members of the committee, the deputy minister and, as his alternate, the assistant deputy minister, and one other person who is not on the staff of the department.
(2) Two members of the committee shall constitute a quorum.

It might be of interest to the house, particularly to those who were not on the committee, if I explained what the real difference is. The original clause provided that the administration of this act should be left to a committee made up of officials of the department. The special committee that considered this bill was of the opinion that there was a certain risk of such a committee becoming more or less political; I do not mean under this government more than under any other government, but it was felt that there was that risk, and the proposal was therefore made and adopted by the committee that an independent committee such as is now proposed should administer the act. While there will still be a representative of the department upon that committee, either the deputy minister or the assistant deputy minister, the other three commissioners, to call them such, will be entirely independent of the department. The object is to ensure that the committee will be independent.

Who will appoint these
commissioners?

The governor in council.
The appointments are political, but not the committee.

What is the underlying
reason for enlarging the personnel of the commission? Is it to exercise further departmental control?

Personally I have not changed my mind in regard to the question of administration. As I explained to the house when I introduced the bill, this is largely a departmental matter and I felt that the administration would be more effective if it were carried on by departmental officials who are now in the department and in the civil service of this country, and who are dealing from day to day with returned soldiers.

War Veterans' Allowances
This would be merely an extension of the work which they are now doing. We have dealt with hospitalization, vocational training, treatment and relief, and vetcraft shops all over Canada for the last twelve years, and there has never been any question of political interference. These officers have always tried to do their work, and taking it all in ail I think that they have done it very well. The opposition members, however, rather objected to a departmental committee, and in the special committee the matter was thoroughly threshed out, and personally I am satisfied to accept the unanimous conclusions of that committee. As regards the deputy minister and the assistant deputy minister, I think that there is a very good reason for including them because we are going to administer this act with the machinery that we now have, and I do not think that it would be wise or that anyone would propose that new machinery should be set up throughout Canada for administration. The services of the Department of Pensions and National Health will have to be given to this independent committee. The idea in associating the deputy minister with the assistant deputy is to give that contact between the department and the committee. I think that is the real explanation in regard to it.

The only objection I see to reducing the quorum from three to two members is that it might be possible for the assistant deputy minister and the additional person, who is not on the staff and is to be named by the governor in council, to constitute themselves a quorum to deal effectively with cases without consulting the other members of the committee. It opens that possibility.

The act specifies the minister or the assistant deputy minister, and there is a fifth member to be chosen by the legion itself. The quorum was reduced from three, as proposed, to two because the commission is composed of three permanent members, and what we had in mind was that two of these could form a quorum.

I wish to move an amendment to section 4, by adding thereto the following subsection:
4 (a). An officer who retires voluntarily after ten years' service and is not pensionable shall receive a refund of all sums deducted from his pay and contributed by him for pension.
Section 5 of the Civil Service Superannuation Act, which is chapter 24 of the Revised Statutes of Canada, provides that a civil servant withdrawing from the service may be given a withdrawal allowance equal to his contributions if he has been in the service ten years or over. Under the existing Militia Pension Act it is the law that officers must contribute 5 per cent of their pay to the pension and retirement fund before becoming pensionable, but if they retire voluntarily their deposits are forfeited. I want to correct that unfair situation. An officer who has served over ten years and who retires voluntarily should receive the amount he paid in.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: The amendment states that section 4 is to be amended, but there are only two sections in the bill.

This refers to section 4 of the existing act. This will have to be a new section of the bill.
Militia Pension Act

My hon. friend was good enough to submit to me a copy of the amendment which he has just moved, and I have had an opportunity to consider it with the officers of the department and to compare the superannuation act with the Militia Pension Act. I know it is my hon. friend's desire to do full justice to those who will be affected by his amendment, and I assure him that I am equally impressed with that duty and that responsibility, but I regret that I must say to him and to the committee that I cannot accept the suggested amendment. In short, his amendment provides that anyone who has served in the permanent force for ten years may voluntarily retire and receive the contributions which he has made towards his pension, and my hon. friend bases his argument on the fact that a civil servant may do the same thing.
I want to point out to my hon. friend in the first place that there is in the Militia Pension Act now a provision that if an officer has served for ten years and by reason of mental or physical incapacity it becomes necessary for him to retire after that period, he is not simply entitled to draw out the amounts he has paid in to the pension fund but is entitled to a gratuity based on a certain scale set out in the act. He is also entitled to compensation if he is retired compulsorily, but I cannot favour permitting officers to enlist and serve for ten years and then, on their own volition, retire to draw out their pension contribution. The reason is quite apparent, as I think the committee will see; a great deal of money is expended by the country on the training of officers in the early stages of their military careers. I do not say they do not give value for the pay they receive, but at the same time it is not in the interests of the service that just when they become useful in connection with the training of other men they should, by reason of some opportunity which may be offered them in commercial life, withdraw with a pecuniary advantage and take up their new occupation having received the benefit of the training they have been given. The position is somewhat different from that of the civil servant.
The other point, upon which I do not wish ;o dwell, is that these two acts are not based on exactly the same principles. There are provisions in the Militia Pension Act which are more favourable to the beneficiaries than are the provisions of the Civil Service Superannuation Act, particularly with regard to the counting of service. So I would ask the hon. member to consider that point when he suggests that these two acts should be put on the same basis. If that is done certain advan-
[Mr. A. E. R.oss.3
tages now accruing to those who come under the Militia Pension Act would have to be given up in compensation for certain advantages which they might receive by having the provisions of the Civil Service Superannuation Act apply. The two acts are not on the same basis and I do not think it would be in the interest of the public service to attempt to put them on the same basis, because we are considering two entirely different sorts of service.

An officer who retires voluntarily after ten years' service and is not pensionable shall receive a refund of all sums deducted from his pay and contributed by him for pension.

I listened with a
great deal of interest to what the minister said, and I think he put the best complexion he could put on the matter. However, there is another side to it which he has not touched. Take the case of an officer who served for ten years, during which time he proved to be unsuited to the service or unfitted for it in some way; the department decides that he is not a useful member of the service and they retire him. He receives what he has contributed to the pension fund.

I think they give him a
gratuity.

The man who is
not fitted for the service gets back his contribution to the pension fund and receives a gratuity as well. On the other hand, a man serves for ten years and proves to be a useful officer; if he desires to take up some other occupation he is let out of the service and his contribution is retained in the fund, while his gratuity is also lost. That is the unfair part of it and that is what I want to correct. Certainly it does not encourage good men to come in if we say, "Well, after ten years you can go out of the service and we will keep the money you have contributed."

I have not discussed this
matter with anyone and really did not understand it until I heard it discussed this afternoon. I do not for one moment question the reasons given by the minister, but at the same time I feel an injustice is done in carrying out the provisions of the act as apparently

Militia Pension Act
they have been carried out in the past and as the minister proposes to continue in the future. After all, the militia officer earns the salary he gets, or is supposed to earn it, at all events. Part of that salary is taken from him as a contribution to the government for the time being, ultimately to be combined with some other money contributed by the government for a pension. It appears to me that really the government is taking his money. He may get some other compensations as the minister suggests; I do not know as to that, but it seems to me the money contributed for pension is distinctly this man's money, and that in justice to him he should get back that money if he feels it necessary for his own advancement or for family reasons to leave the service. While this is the first time I have heard this question discussed, on a number of occasions I have learned of similar regulations in other branches of the service, where men have made contributions to the pension fund and have not been allowed to get back their money. I think these men should receive that money in all cases, because it is their money. Without going further into the question I think the hon. member for Kingston is on very solid ground, and I should like to see t'he minister concede the point, which seems only just.

I fully appreciate the
arguments of the hon. members for Fort William (Mr. Manion) and Kingston (Mr. Ross). If their contention is correct, it means that the money deducted from an officer's pay is still his money. Everyone admits that it is not his money if he has had for instance only eight years of service. In that case that money remains in the common pool for the payment of pensions. This money does not become the officer's until such time expires as under the act entitles him to receive a pension. It is nothing less than group insurance. I understand the hon. member for Kingston desires to make it a little easier for the man to get that money back, but I think he understands much better than I do, having been in the service for a longer period, that a man should not be allowed voluntarily to withdraw from the service with a financial advantage. I do not think he should be allowed to take his pension contribution unless he has completed the term of service provided for in the act.
If a man is found to be unsuitable, I can assure my hon. friend that we will not wait until he has completed ten years of service before discharging him. If a man is unsuitable it will be probably found out within five years, in which case there would be no reward 2419-109
paid such as is suggested by the hon. member for Kingston. Another point is this: a pension is in lieu of employability; it is for the purpose of providing for the man who is not otherwise employable. A man who has spent time in the service and is unemployable perhaps is more entitled to a pension than the man who may be perfectly independent in every way but who simply leaves the service to better his own position in life.
In the interests of the service I cannot accept my hon. friend's amendment.

I think the hon. minister is quite sincere, but I do not agree with him that this thing is 100 per cent agreeable to all the officers in the service. I cannot agree with his statement that advantage has not been taken of this clause and of other amendments which have been added to the Pension Act. Favours have been granted to those who, in the opinion of the minister of the department-I do not refer to the present minister-were not entitled to them. I think it is fair to a man who has given ten years of service that he should receive back only the money he has contributed without any interest.

The officers and men of the permanent force are, after all, civil servants; they are in the employ of the government and of the country. The amendment moved by the hon. member for Kingston (Mr. Ross) simply seeks to give the retired officer who has put in ten years of service the same rights granted to other civil servants who retire voluntarily. The member of the permanent force should have the right when he leaves the service to withdraw the deposit which he has made towards superannuation or pension, whatever you choose to call it. It seems to me vastly unfair to discriminate against the members of the permanent force. From year to year they have put lip 5 per cent of their salaries, and when they choose to retire that should be returned to them. During times of peace their retirement would not cripple the service, as it would be an easy matter to replace them, and it seems to me to be only equitable that they should be allowed to withdraw the deposits they have made.

I know of one man who put in ten years of service and was then retired. He accepted a position in Ottawa, and the pension board said to him: Your pay cannot go higher than a certain amount because you have retired. There are many things contained in this act which are unfair, and I think the minister should endeavour to

Militia Pension Act

correct them. The minister knows of this case officially, that the man cannot get more than what he retires on.
It is the other way.
That he can get more?
Yes.
I was given to understand that he could not.

His pension and salary
could be more than what he is retired on.
I have no desire to press the matter unduly, but it seems to me that a man who has been in the service for ten years, and then withdraws should not suffer financial disadvantage.
He should not have any advantage.

He loses the money which he has donated and thus suffers a pecuniary disadvantage. Withdrawal from the service is generally an effort on the man's part to better his position, and if he remains he suffers a pecuniary disadvantage. If he leaves, he also suffers a pecuniary disadvantage, so he gets it, coming and going. I do not say it in any offensive way, but it seems as though the dice are loaded against him.
He cannot lose anything until it is due him, and it is not due him until it accrues according to the provisions of the act.

It is a part of his salary
which has been taken over as pension and kept by the government.
He does not lose it when he leaves the service; he lost it when the deduction was made.
He loses it once ihe gives up his position.
He cannot get it back until he completes the term provided for by the act.
It is his until he leaves the service.
What is that term?

Twenty years at least under ordinary circumstances. If he is retired compulsorily or forced to retire by physical or mental infirmity, the period is ten years. I have not the act before me, but I believe that in the latter case he receives as well a certain gratuity.

Does the minister know of other civil servants who are treated in this way? Assume that a man is receiving $4,000 per year, the 5 per cent deduction would amount to $200 annually. A man may have been eight years in the service and have an opportunity to better his position, but he cannot do so except at a loss. Let me put it in this way: he has paid the money to the government. It is true it is a deduction, but nevertheless his salary is $4,000, and this is kept off for a specific purpose, namely, to provide for pension. After eight years' service we find that this man has $1,600 to his credit. It may be assumed that he has given faithful service during that period or he would have been dismissed. He has no redress whatever. In an ordinary insurance company any time after you have paid premiums for three years, your policy has a loan value or a cash surrender value. Why in the world is such a tremendous deduction made in this case and a man put in the position that he has to remain in the service for twenty years or lose the whole thing? I suppose after all the justice or injustice of it would depend upon what knowledge the man has of his contract when he enters the service I do not know whether or not any special pains are taken to let men know exactly the terms on which they are joining or whether such information appears on the application or not. Could the minister let us know whether one joining the service signs an application which makes this quite plain at the time? If not, it seems to me a great injustice and I cannot help thinking the amendment of the hon. member for Kingston is most appropriate.

I thought I made the point clear and I do not want to labour it. Does my hon. friend know that every civil servant serving in this department and every other department for eight years is in exactly the same position?
I was given to understand they were not.

A civil servant has to serve ten years before he gets anything back. It is not regarded as an injustice; it is only part of an insurance fund. The point is that the hon. member for Kingston is trying to lessen the period and I do not think my hon. friend understood this when he asked whether any other department did this. Every department of government has the same rule. I will read the section of the Civil Service Superannuation Act:
5. The governor in council may grant to any contributor who has served in the civil service for ten years or upwards and .... who for

Militia Pension Act
any reason other than misconduct or those hereinbefore specified retires, whether voluntarily or by dismissal or removal, from the civil service, a withdrawal allowance payable in one sum equal to the total amount of his contributions made under this act without interest.
I do not want my hon. friend to single out the department over which I happen to preside.
Do not make it personal.

I am not trying to make it personal, but I do not want him to single out this department as being one which does something which somebody calls grossly unfair. The same thing is done in every department. What the hon. member for Kingston is asking is that at the end of ten years a man in the military service shall be entitled to voluntary retirement and shall get back that money. I have pointed out that the civil service is different from the military service. A great deal of money is spent by this country in training officers in order that they may be able to perform their duties efficiently. Is it in the public interest to have them enter, say the engineering service, give them a training which is very valuable in civil life, and then have them say: Give me my money back and I will go into civil life? There are certain cases in which this act is more beneficial to officers than the Civil Service Superannuation Act is to civil service employees.
Will the minister explain why?

There is the counting of time served for pension. Nonpermanent militia service, war service, permanent force service count under this. All these things which are in the government service count toward pension, whereas a civil service employee could be in the militia for several years and then enter the civil service, and his militia service would not count for pension. I do not think it is in the interest of the service or of the individual that we should enter into a discussion or a comparison of the benefits under the two acts, because in some respects and in certain cases the Civil Service Superannuation Act is better for some individuals and in certain cases and in some respects the Militia Pension Act is better for some individuals. In certain cases, I ask the committee to remember this: this has been in force since 1900 in any case and it seems to have worked well. I have no doubt there are individual cases in which they feel they would like to leave the service and take their contribution. I have had one or perhaps two my-2419-109}
self, in which they would like to do this, but it has not been regarded as being in the interests of the service. The provision seems to have worked satisfactorily and I feel that the act, in view of the experience we have had, can be allowed to remain as it stands.
In what respect would this not be in the interests of the service? How would it injure the service?

If my hon. friend had in a special business an employee under contract for say twenty years whom he had trained for years and on whose training he has spent a great deal of money, does he not think it would injure the business if that employee, who was under contract for twenty years, were able to put on his hat and say: "I am leaving now; give me the money I have paid in." That is the reason it is not in the interests of the service. The hon. member for Kingston says that all officers were not in favour of my proposition. I can quite understand that. If 1 were an officer, I would not be in favour of it either; I would hope the provisions would be as favourable as possible. But one has to remember one's responsibilities in conducting a department and one has to remember the history and the way in which these matters have been worked out. It has been found satisfactory in the past, and I ask the committee to accept my suggestion that the amendment be not pressed. I quite understand that my hon. friend may not agree with me, but it is my point of view backed up by my officers who have had experience in these matters.

While perhaps I
should abide by the minister's request as this is a house of responsibility and he has a department under him, I did differ from him in saying it was not one hundred per cent satisfactory. I honestly believe he would get better officers if it were known that after ten years' service they could retire voluntarily without having to be shoved out for mental incapacity or physical disability or something of that kind, or else put into another job at another salary before getting what was due to them. I do not believe the service would suffer at all if this were done. All I want to point out is that these are men who are fitted for service in civil life; they have remained in the government service for ten years and all they ask is not the gratuity but the cash contribution.
This is in line with what we have been doing in life insurance.	For years life
insurance was conducted in a way that compelled men to contribute year after year and
Militia Pension Act

if by a little slip or for some other reason they failed to pay up for one year, they lost all they had contributed. That has all been corrected in life insurance and I do not believe the militia department would suffer one iota if they said: This man has given ten years' good, faithful service; we are willing for him to retire, but we will not give him a gratuity, we will give him simply the cash we have deducted from his salary without interest. If the minister feels that this cannot be accepted, I have no alternative than to withdraw for the time being the amendment, but I certainly believe I am on grounds of simple, British justice.

I asked the minister to
give the advantages that the officers in this department obtained. He gave as the outstanding advantage that an officer who, for instance, had served o%'erseas for some years, got credit for that service when it came to the matter of pension, whereas this was not the case in the other branches of the civil service. Of course there is an obvious answer to that, namely, that the man who has served overseas has had the very finest kind of training for an officer of this kind, whereas he would not necessarily have any training that would be of use in some other branches of the civil service. So far as I can see that is not an advantage of any importance to the officers. That was the main argument of the minister.

I did not give it as an
outstanding example. I just happened to have it noted. I do not think it is to the benefit of individuals to indulge in a comparison of the two acts. That is what I am advised by my officers. I have not gone into every detail, but I am informed that there are substantial advantages under this act. I do not think it is well for us to say that we are going to put it on all fours with the Civil Service Superannuation Act.
Amendment withdrawn.

I have another
amendment. I move that there be added to this bill a clause 3, which will amend section 8 of the Militia Pension Act, paragraph (f), which reads:
The time served as an officer, non-commissioned officer or man on active service during the war between Great Britain and Germany which commenced on the fourth day of August, one thousand nine hundred and fourteen.
I feel that that ought to be interpreted to include one who served in any part of that war, but on the contrary I find that certain splendid non-commissioned officers who had

retired from the permanent force on pension perhaps a year or two before war was declared were induced to come back for the purpose of training troops, and when they came back they offered themselves for overseas service, but they were forced to remain in Canada for the purpose of training troops during the four years of the war. They had had experience as artillery officers, and they were retained in Canada contrary to their own wishes, almost by compulsion, you might say, during those four years. Those who went overseas had these four years added to their service, which gives a proportional increase in their pension. I am asking that this section shall apply to these non-commissioned officers formerly of the permanent corps who were forcibly retained in Canada during the four years of the war for the purpose of giving training, and I therefore move to add the following words to paragraph (f), "including the time so served in Canada."
Would the hon. member read the clause as it would be as amended?

I should really have to read the whole section. Section 8 deals with the time that may be included in the term of service and includes time served with the military forces in South Africa, time served by an officer of the Canadian militia with the South African constabulary, time served with the Royal Canadian regiment at Halifax, and so on, and then paragraph (f) says:
The time served as an officer, non-commissioned officer or man on active service during the war between Great Britain and Germany.
My amendment is to add to that paragraph the words " including the time so served in Canada." That will simply mean that they will get the four years that they served in Canada added to their permanent corps service for pension purposes. Nobody can deny that the four years they gave in Canada should be so considered. These men sacrificed very much, after taking a small pension, in the one case, I think, of $25, they came back to give their services, and they gave excellent service in the way of training men for the war, and yet that four years' service has not been counted. There are not very many of them. I think I know only about four peramnent non-commissioned officers in this class, who retired only a year or two before the war was declared, and then came back and gave excellent service, and yet they have been refused this additional time for pension purposes. I think it is only fair that they should be considered, and that those words should be added.

Militia Pension Act

My hon. friend has been
kind enough to call this matter to my attention and to submit to me a copy of his amendment. Both these cases are illustrative of the maxim well known to lawyers, that hard cases make bad laws. My hon. friend no doubt has some specific cases in mind of a man who served in the permanent force, and retired before the war, drawing a pension from the permanent force. The call comes for men to enlist for Canadian expeditionary force service. One man after he has retired from the permanent force and has become a civilian and is drawing a pension enlists and serves either overseas or in Canada. Another man who has not served in the permanent force also enlists and serves, and what my hon. friend suggests is that the man who served in the permanent force and had become a civilian to all intents and purposes the same as the man who enlisted for the first time shall receive an award for serving in the Canadian expeditionary force in addition to his permanent force pension. In other words, the man who enlisted de novo, not having served before, gets a war service gratuity, and that is all he gets for his Canadian expeditionary force service; but the permanent force man, under my hon. friend's amendment, is to get an additional award, if I might put it that way, by way of an addition to his permanent force pension. Let me say to my hon. friend-I expect that he remembers it far better than I do-that this whole case was threshed out by the parliamentary committee presided over by Mr. Hume Cronyn and I understand that at that time a recommendation was made to the effect that the case of one man should not be any different from the other, that their Canadian expeditionary force service should be exactly on the same basis, that the permanent force man who had retired and then enlisted should not have his pension increased by the fact that he subsequently served during the war either overseas or in Canada. I feel that the decision made at that time was sound, and I am sorry that here again I cannot assist my hon. friend in the one or two cases that he has in mind.

Has the man not
retired prior to the war, either voluntarily or compulsorily, then the time that he served in Canada or elsewhere during the war would have counted for pension. The mere fact that he retired from the permanent force, probably compulsorily, and then comes back -for the war and does additional service, surely should not be counted against him.
It is not counted against him.

That is the fact.
Suppose a non-commissioned officer had continued to serve in the permanent force during the war, the full time put in by him would count for pension, but merely because he was out of the permanent force for perhaps a week before the wa.r began and his services were again required, he should not have his pension reduced. If you will look at section 8 of the Militia Pension Act, you will see that the following times may also be included in the term of service of an officer for the purposes of this act; (a) time served with the military service in South Africa; (b) time served by an officer of the Canadian militia with the South African constabulary; (c) time served with the third battalion of the Royal Canadian regiment of infantry at Halifax; (d) time served with the Yukon field force in any one or more of the years 1898, 1899 and 1900. Why the time served with the Yukon field force should count I am quite at a loss to know, because it was an absolute waste of -money sending that force up to the Yukon. They went there on a joy ride, and it -continued as a joy ride all the time that they were there.

They were still
non-commissioned officers of the permanent force while serving with the Yukon field force. There was continuity of service.
True.
There was continuity of service. That is the basis of the act.

Supposing there was a break in the service of any of these officers or non-commissioned officers who went back into the Yukon field force, this bill would not cover them, just as in the case the hon. member for Kingston has in mind in moving this amendment. It seems to me unfair discrimination.

Mr. Chairman,
neither the minister nor the former deputy will deny that when the men joined the Canadian expeditionary force they broke their service with the permanent force.
No.

Yes, they broke
their service and had to be taken on again.

Will you allow me a
second to explain?

I have the floor,
Mr. Former Deputy Minister. That man's pension of twenty-five dollars should not be affected; he has earned it, it is his right. Now, this case is dissimilar from the other one. In the former case he had not earned his pension,
\

Militia Pension Act
but in this case he has. Yet you say that because he has earned it you are not going to give him anything further. But because some officers first went out to South Africa they did get that service. Surely the former deputy minister cannot say that they did not break their service when they joined the South African constabulary.

They were in the
permanent force then.

But will you say
these officers who joined the South African constabulary did not break their service?
They did not break their service.

They did; they
came back and rejoined the service in Canada. There was just as much a break in the service of the men who joined the South African constabulary after the war was over and remained there for two or three years and then came back into the service here as there was in the case of the men who had gone out of the permanent force and came back into it again. I think you have made your position very ridiculous in trying to say that there is no break there. I am fighting for two ordinary non-commissioned officers, to see that their time is dealt with on the same basis as that of some officers who joined the South African constabulary. I do not intend to withdraw this amendment; I am going to press it.

As I told my hon. friend, the matter has all been thrashed out before a committee of this house and thoroughly considered. I do not think he realizes how far-reaching this amendment is. Those who enlisted in the Canadian expeditionary force after having been retired and being in civil life are all put on the same basis. That is the principle on which the former committee went, and it is the principle for which I have to stand as advised by my officers.

Will the minister
then explain-

I am not explaining at
all with regard to the act, I am dealing with the case which my hon. friend is submitting. There are a good many cases which would not be regarded at all if the men were in the civil service. They are given the benefit of it here. I do not think it serves the purpose of those who are interested in the Militia Pension Act to bring these cases up. I have introduced this amendment for the benefit of certain widows who, it is pointed

out, do not get the consideration which the law officers of the crown thought they were intended to get. I felt that they should be benefited. I do submit to my hon. friend that the bringing into this discussion of two cases that have nothing to do with the subject matter does not help us at all, and it makes us feel inclined not to introduce any further amendments to the Militia Pension Act. I would get along beautifully if I did not introduce any amendments at all, but when I try to make this amendment my hon. friend goes over the whole act to try to find some place where more generous provision is made than in the two cases he has in mind. As I have said, hard cases make bad laws. There may be cases such as he has in mind where small pensions have been granted, but the general principle is sound, and it has been accepted by a parliamentary committee and by parliament itself. I ask my hon. friend whether it is in the interest of the people for whom this act was passed for him to press this amendment.

I think it is
justified by the mere fact that we come up here session after session and find that some special case is introduced. Now, I consider that my case is just as meritorious as the one brought up by the minister, and that it is just as meritorious as the one he brought up last session. As long as that is done because of some person at headquarters here or by some one with a little bit of "pull," to obtain these special favours, I am going, as I gave warning to the minister last year, to bring up these meritorious cases.

If my hon. friend suggests that this bill is introduced because of anybody at headquarters or because of someone else who has "pull," he is very much mistaken. It has been introduced for the reason I have already stated. If my hon. friend is determined to press his amendment, I think it will be best for the committee to rise and report progress.

That is the same
kind of threat as the minister made last year. I am not saying a word against his case, but I am asking for similar consideration for another meritorious case.
My hon. friend-

I have the floor
and I intend to keep it. Surely the minister is a bigger man than to threaten to withdraw a favour which has not been contested by me.

Department of Marine

Will my hon. friend
permit me? I understood him to say-he will correct me if I am wrong-that this case which I have presented, and which he says is no more meritorious than his, had been presented because of "pull" exercised by somebody at headquarters. If that is the case,
I	can assure him the "pull" will cease right here, and I will ask the committee to rise and report progress.

I said that time
after time we have seen cases brought up here in favour of some person, but I was not speaking against this particular case; I simply said that my case was as meritorious as the minister's. I do not think the minister, after the gallant service that he has given, will say that because I am pressing for a favour for a meritorious case, he is going to withdraw this favour to some poor widow, a favour which I am not opposing in any way.
No.

If it will help his
widow to get this favour I will withdraw my amendment.

Right Hon. W. L. MACKENZIE KING (Prime Minister) moved that the house go into committee to consider the following proposed resolution:
That it is expedient to provide that there shall be a Department of Marine, presided over by a minister of the crown; that the powers and duties of the minister be defined, and provision made for the appointment of a deputy minister and the employment of such other officers, clerks and employees as may be deemed necessary.
Motion agreed to and the house went into committee, Mr. Marcil in the chair.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subsubtopic: PROVISION FOR SEPARATE DEPARTMENT PRESIDED OVER BY A MINISTER
speechtext:
As members
of the house are aware, there is at the present time a Department of Marine and Fisheries. The purpose of the bill which is based on the present resolution and which will be introduced is to divide the present Department of Marine and Fisheries into two departments, a Department of Marine and a. Department of
Fisheries. For some time past it has been felt that the fisheries resources of this country should receive the attention of a separate ministry. Canada is rich in her natural resources of agriculture, fisheries, lumbering, mining and power. From the point of view of value, it is believed that the fisheries resources are second in the list of natural resources. As compared with the fisheries resources of other countries of the world, we have in our deep sea and inland fisheries the largest and most valuable anywhere to be found. During the past ten years there have been no less than three royal commissions each of which has concerned itself in whole or in part with waters pertaining to Canadian fisheries. The first commission was appointed in 1922, and was composed entirely of hon. members of this house. It was appointed to inquire into the fisheries of British Columbia. In 1926 the royal commission on maritime claims considered, amongst others, the representations of the maritime provinces in respect to the fisheries industry.

subsubtopic: PROVISION FOR SEPARATE DEPARTMENT PRESIDED OVER BY A MINISTER
speechtext:
Did the Duncan
report recommend a separate ministry or a separate department?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subsubtopic: PROVISION FOR SEPARATE DEPARTMENT PRESIDED OVER BY A MINISTER
speechtext:
I will come to that in a minute. In 1928 a royal commission appointed to investigate the fisheries of the maritime provinces and the Magdalen Islands made its report. The commissioners were: the Hon. A. K. Maclean, and Messrs. Cyrus Macmillan, H. R, L. Bill, Joseph Mombour-quette and J. C. Robichaud. AH three commissions were concerned, as I have said, with the question of Canadian fisheries. Two of them were concerned exclusively with fisheries, one with those on the Pacific coast, and the other with those on the Atlantic coast.
My hon. friend the member for Argenteuil (Sir George Perley) asked if the Duncan commission recommended the appointment of a separate minister. The report of that commission recommended the establishment of two main branches of the Department of Marine and Fisheries, the two branches to be placed under separate deputy heads, one to deal with marine matters and the other with fisheries. The commission which reported in 1928 went however, a step farther. It recommended that there should be a separate ministry of fisheries created. I shall read the recommendation of that commission as it is found at page 82 of the report:
Numerous representations [DOT]were made to us on the necessity for the establishment of a separate ministry of fisheries. It was pointed out that a separate Department of Fisheries would elevate the industry in importance, would
Department of Marine

stimulate a greater public interest in its special problems, and would permit of undivided administrative attention, thereby ensuring a more extensive and complete organization. The suggestion was also made that with the extensive fisheries of the Atlantic and Pacific coasts, and such of the inland fisheries as are under federal control, there is a sufficiently large field for administrative work in the future to justify the creation of a separate ministry. It was contended that the Department of Marine and Fisheries has so wide a jurisdiction and such a variety of problems, that, as at present organized, it is unable to devote sufficient time to fishery matters.
Much can be said in support of this view. The fishing industry is territorially widespread on both the Atlantic and Pacific coasts, each area having difficulties that are dissimilar from those of the other. It is great in variety, in extent and in value; it holds a very large place in the economic life of the country; and in all phases it is beset with complex problems of administration. The industry may, therefore, justly claim to be of such importance as to require a separate ministry. Last year, parliament authorized the appointment of a Deputy Minister of Fisheries. We found throughout the maritime provinces a widespread feeling not only in support of this action, but also in support of the establishment of a separate Department of Fisheries under a Minister of Fisheries, and we recommend the creation of such a department to the consideration of the government of Canada.
At the time that effect was given to the recommendation contained in the Duncan report for the establishment of two deputy heads to the branches of marine and of fisheries respectivefiy, I indicated that in all probability the government would appoint at a later date a separate minister of fisheries. Perhaps at this time I should say that when the two departments are separated, it is contemplated to effect a measure of reorganization in regard to the work of some of the other departments. We believe such a reorganization would be very much in the interests of the country. For example, to-day dredging of rivers and harbours is carried on largely by the Department of Public Works; it is also carried on to some extent by the Department of Railways and Canals. The government has felt that from the point of view of efficiency and economy a much needed improvement would be effected if the work of dredging were concentrated in the department which deals more particularly with marine affairs. At a later time there will accordingly be a reorganization of the marine department along lines which will enlarge the work of that department in this and other particulars. That department will be able to give its attention more exclusively to marine affairs, while to the very important phases of the fisheries industry it will be possible to give much more in the way of attention by having those matters placed under a 
separate minister. That is the purpose of the present legislation.

subsubtopic: PROVISION FOR SEPARATE DEPARTMENT PRESIDED OVER BY A MINISTER
speechtext: I certainly am not going to object to this proposed legislation, but I would like to call the attention of the Prime Minister to the report of the Duncan commission, which does not call for a separate minister. Fisheries are a most important part of our national life, but I have felt strongly for years that we have more ministers in Canada than we require. Whether or not there should be a separate Minister of Fisheries is beside the question at the moment, but this will add one more to the number. In the years I have been in public life it has seemed to me that we should get on with fewer ministers. It is true that the duties of the different members of the cabinet vary a great deal; some of them have a great deal to do while others have comparatively little, but here we have a country of ten million people with seventeen ministers at full salary. We all know that the United States gets along with only seven ministers.

speechtext: I am not arguing that we should follow the example of the United States; far from it, but I am saying that great country gets on with comparatively few ministers. It seems to me it would be easier for the Prime Minister and for the cabinet to discuss public questions if there were not so many of them. I am not going to object in any way to the creation of a Department of Fisheries, which I think is perfectly proper, but I do not think we should add to the number of cabinet ministers we have now. It is very easy to add to the number and very hard to take away from it, as the Prime Minister knows. If you make an addition now, who knows when we will have a man in the Prime Minister's chair who will reduce the number as it seems to me it should be reduced? I object to increasing the present number of ministers.

promise my hon. friend that the number will not be increased. As he is aware, in this house we have passed to-day enactments under which the natural resources of the three western provinces must be transferred to those provinces, as well as certain lands to the province of British Columbia. When that transfer is effected it should be possible to do away entirely with the ministry of the interior. Some reorganization and consolidation will be effected as respects the Department of Immigration, the Department of Indian Affairs, the forestry service and allied branches of the public service. At present the Minister of the Interior, I believe, is acting minister as well for two or three departments; I hope it will not be necessary to have any acting minister in the future but to have one minister to whom may be entrusted the administration of these several branches. The intention being to drop one minister almost immediately, I hope my hon. friend will feel reassured as to the present measures not involving any increase in the total number of ministers.
Since my hon. friend referred to the United States, I might remind the committee that the ministers in the United States are engaged exclusively in executive work, with no responsibility to congress. We certainly could get along with a much smaller number of ministers in Canada if our ministers did not have to spend so much time in parliament, and I quite agree with my hon. friend that a small meeting of council is easier to handle than a large meeting.

The most convenient and effective procedure appears to be that of creating two new departments. Under one of the provisions of the Interpretation Act the officials of the old department are automatically reappointed.

speechtext: It is somewhat consoling for us to learn that the minister, or rather the ministry of the interior is to be dropped. It has been urged that the United States gets along with fewer ministers than we have, and the Prime Minister has replied that the ministers in the United States have not the parliamentary work to do. We might also remember that in England they do not require quite so many ministers as we have, but they have a system whereby undersecretaries do a certain amount of the parliamentary work. I do not see why we could not adopt a similar system here, and instead of having a full time minister on full pay we might have some of the younger members of the house, who perhaps might be ambitious to find a place in the cabinet some day, get their training by undertaking the parliamentary end of the work. I have a complaint to make in this particular regard. I am appealing at the present time, not for the higher paid but for the lower paid men. As well as receiving low wages, they have a 5 per cent deduction for the civil service superannuation fund. This

means that many men who enter the postal service start at a wage of about $85 a month. They have to pass a very thorough examination; they must be men even above the average. The government having been so considerate of the higher paid men as to go to the extent of appointing a commission to investigate their salaries, the commission having reported favourably and, I understand, the government having decided to accept to some extent the recommendations of the commission, I am surprised that they are doing nothing for the lower paid men. I want to know whether it is possible for the government to do for the lower paid men, particularly those in the postal service, exactly what they have done for the higher paid men. I appeal to the Postmaster General to say that he will appoint a committee or commission of some kind to investigate the salaries of the lower paid men under his jurisdiction.

Beginning at $1,020, the postal helper goes up to $1,320, which is the maximum, so after three or more years' service they receive the maximum of $1,320. Of course, the postal clerks start at a higher minimum; I believe it is about 81,200, although I have not the exact figure at hand. I am not contending that they are paid too much or that they get enough.
I merely wish to point out that when hon. members speak of postal helpers drawing less than $100 a month, there is a short period during which they do receive less than 8100 a month, but it is not very long before they are receiving more than $100 a month.
Does the minister think that anything around $100 a month, even $115, is a living wage under conditions that prevail in Canada to-day?

I am not in a position to express an opinion upon that just now, but I

The impression prevails that these men remain at that salary. They do not. They go as high in that class as a maximum of $1,320. Then there is the opportunity for promotion from postal helper to postal clerk, and so forth, and as they advance to these higher grades the salary increases to $1,800 and $2,100, but they must begin at the bottom of the ladder. I am not going to offer what I am now about to say as an excuse for low wages, but let me draw attention to this fact, that every time the Civil Service Commission advertises for applicants for these lower grades, we have more applicants than we can handle.

I do not see how we can justify a public utility such as our post office in paying such low wages. I think the people of the Dominion would rather sooner pay a little more for the postal service than see the men receiving these low wages. I do not think there is any credit coming to the postal department in reducing the cost of the services and at the same time paying low wages to the men performing those services. They enter the service at a minimum of $1,080 for the first year; the next year it increases to $1,200 and the next year to $1,320. These figures apply to letter carriers. There is an annual increase of $120. The maximum is reached in the fifth year and it is only during the first year that the employees receive less than $100 per month.
I thought the increase was $60 a year.

It is $120.
