speechtext: When the committee rose at six o'clock we were considering vote No. 299, which is to be found on page 70 of the estimates.

When the committee rose at six o'clock we were discussing the question of salaries. The minister gave the committee the number of employees in the lower grades who received below $100 per month. He gave various figures, including 770 in the lowest grade and 800 in the next grade.
The total was 4,403.
Who were getting under $100 per month.

Before the committee rose at six o'clock I gave the following figures:
Letter carriers	2,763
Mail porters	 770
Postal helpers	 870
Total	4,403
Supply-Post Office

The annual increase amounts to $120, so that in five years they would be receiving around $1,600. It must not be understood that the total number of 4,403 are receiving only $1,020.
Could the minister tell the committee how many are receiving that salary?
As far as I can find out, the average would be from 20 to 25 per cent.
Could the minister give a rough estimate of how many are receiving under $100 per month?
At the present time there are not more than 20 per cent of the 4,403 receiving the minimum of $1,020.

I would like to say a few words along the lines taken by the hon. member for North Winnipeg (Mr. Heaps). There are some hundreds of men receiving $100 per month or less. The minister pointed out last year, and has pointed out again this year

I believe he mentioned it two years ago as well -that the Civil Service Commission has recommended against any increase, and therefore that he is more or less helpless. I have no desire to question the word of the minister, and I do not do it in any offensive way, but it would seem to be obvious that if the minister and the government desired to increase the wages paid to these men in the lower grades, this House of Commons would support such a measure. It does not seem fair that the minister should place the whole responsibility upon the Civil Service Commission. This government has a statistical department which has issued figures showing that the cost of living for the average family in Canada is considerably more than the minimum paid to these men. In view of that fact, it would seem to me that the government might well set an example to the private employers and make a ruling which the Civil Service Commission would have to obey, or bring a resolution before the house. If that were done, I am sure the minister would receive the support of the whole house. The fact that the minister argued that there were many private corporations paying similar salaries is really no argument, because-
I did not make that argument.
Somebody did.
It was the Minister of the Interior (Mr. Stewart).

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior
speechtext:
I said that
that was the basis upon which the Civil Service Commission fixed the salaries, in comparison with the remuneration paid for work of. a similar character.

I thought it was the Postmaster General who had made that statement. The fact that private corporations pay a smaller salary is all the more reason why the government should set a good example. I do not think either the people of this country or the members of this house believe the minister to be absolutely sincere in this matter. He has taken the attitude that he is helpless before the Civil Service Commission, when in fact the government could bring in a resolution which would have the effect of forcing that commission to raise the salaries of these men.

Mr. Chairman, I
would like to add a few words in support of what has been said by the hon. member for Fort William (Mr. Manion) and by my colleague. The minister objected to the use of the word "dodging" by an hon. member, but it would appear that he is hiding behind the Civil Service Commission, because he has told us again and again that they are the ones who are responsible. When we ask him what he has done, he simply replies that he has asked what the Civil Service Commission has done. It seems to me that he is the one really responsible in this matter. The Civil Service Commission was not set up in order to control parliament; parliament is here to control the Civil Service Commission, and parliament has a right to look to the minister and to the government to introduce such legislation as will meet the needs of this case.
As has been pointed out to-night, there is no reason why legislation could not be introduced which would provide the minimum asked for, that is, at least $100 per month. If we stipulate that corporations having contracts with the government pay fair and adequate wages, there is no reason why the Postmaster General (Mr. Veniot) should not introduce such legislation as would ensure the employees of his department receiving an adequate and reasonable wage. The minister himself admits that this is not a living wage. If that is so, why does he not introduce this legislation, and introduce it at this session?
I cannot conceive, in view of what has been said, of objection being raised by hon. members on this side of the house. The Postmaster General must be held responsible for the low wages being paid to his employees.

Supply-Post Office
The Postmaster General has referred to the large number of applicants for the different positions. He contends that that is not the reason for the low wages, but why should it be referred to unless as an excuse? We have been told by the Prime Minister that the policy of his government is not to consider labour as a commodity; it should not be bought and sold subject to the fluctuations in the market. In spite of that statement by the Prime Minister, the Postmaster General apparently considers that wages can be kept down just so long as there are a large number of people seeking positions.
That is certainly a wrong interpretation of what I said.
It is an inference, not an interpretation.
The hon. member has no grounds for such an inference.
I think the house must judge of that. When the minister has it within his own power
He has not.

-to introduce legislation that will give a living wage and he refuses to exercise that power, and when he reminds the house that there are large numbers of people who are anxious to get jobs, what does that mean if not what I say? The minister does not tell us what it means. I think, as my colleague pointed out, that the number of applications is in itself an indication of the large amount of unemployment in the country, because ordinarily people would not accept $100 and less a month if permanent jobs at reasonable wages were being offered throughout Canada. While this situation indicates the large amount of unemployment, it is no excuse for our squeezing men because we find them on the verge of the bread line.
Reference has also been made to the low salaries paid to bank employees. We all know that the salaries paid to junior clerks in banks are nothing less than a scandal. The minister himself would have to admit that, but why drag that in as an excuse for the Dominion government paying low wages?
The Beatty report, to which reference has been made, makes this statement:
Having in mind the obvious desire of the government as indicated by the reference to us, to improve the status of its technical officers with a view to increasing the efficiency of that 2419-110
branch of the service, it has occurred to us that an investigation of the civil service generally, that is. as to numbers, nature of work and rates of pay. might conceivably result in some economy and greater efficiency.
The Beatty report itself suggests this wider review of the situation. I cannot see why the minister should not follow up such a recommendation as this with regard not merely to the higher paid but also to the lower paid employees in the civil service. In a communication that I received a short time ago from the Amalgamated Civil Servants of Canada, I find the following statement:
That to increase the salaries of the nearly
4,000	employees who were stated to be male adults receiving less than $1,200 per annum to that figure, would entail an extra cost of only $765,000 annually.
If this figure is correct, we have the figure that the hon. member for Fort William has been looking for. There are about 4,000 who are receiving under $100 a month.
Will the hon. member permit me to correct him? There are fewer than 4,000 receiving $100 a month. Out of that 4,403 mentioned, there would not be more than 20 per cent receiving under $100 a month.
The hon. member means the whole service.
I am referring to the postal service in regard to what the hon. member for Fort William has said.

The hon. member for Fort William was trying to get some figures
and I was giving it on the authority of the Amalgamated Civil Servants of Canada that altogether some 4,000 civil service employees are receiving $100 or less a month. Is that figure approximately correct?
I cannot speak for the other departments; I can speak only for my own.

I am considering the larger question. As a matter of fact, the sum mentioned is only, by the most conservative estimate, one and one-half per cent of the civil service salary list.
The statement continues:
Civil servants' salaries generally have by no means kept pace with those of workers in the important classes of the industrial world. We find from a study of the government's own publications that the wages and salaries of the latter class have, since 1913, advanced approximately 88 per cent, while the former have advanced only 64 per cent. Cost of living figures have risen as high as the latter figure, so that the standard of living of civil servants is, as a matter of course, far below that of his coworkers of outside employ.

Supply-Post Office

Let me come back, in closing, specifically to the post office workers. I find in the statements presented yesterday by the Minister of Finance that the post office revenue for 192829 was 830,611,964, and the estimated revenue for 1929-30 is $33,346,000. Since the post office is such a large revenue bearing department of government, I think I am right in saying the only revenue bearing department, and since we have such large sums coming in, due no doubt not merely to the monopoly that exists but also to a considerable extent to the efficiency of the service rendered by large numbers of these comparatively low paid workers, the least that can be done under that circumstance is to ensure that those workers obtain a decent living wage. We can urge only, as we have done year after year, as the civil servants themselves have done for some ten years, that their salary shall be put on the basis of a reasonable wage. I ask the minister whether he can see his way clear this session to overcome any opposition which he says exists on the part of the Civil Service Commission, by introducing legislation that will establish a minimum wage based upon the cost of living.

I wish to add a word
to what has just been said. It is strange that this readjustment of salaries should have had to be asked for during several consecutive sessions. When we consider the responsibilities of the postal workers and the character of the service they render, is it fair to ask them to work for $90 or less a month? They are looked upon in every home in Canada as messengers of good will. They bear tidings, sometimes of joy and sometimes of regret. Why should the house demur to the proposal that at least $100 a- month be paid to the postal employees? I am not going to ask the house to compare them with United States postal employees, because if I did the Prime Minister would say: We turn to Westminster and not to Washington. But I submit that they are underpaid, they are certainly inadequately paid for the work they do and the responsibility they have to assume. I wish to concur in the sentiments expressed by hon. members who have spoken in this connection. We should raise the minimum salary for postal workers to $100 a month. I hope the Postmaster General will consider the matter, and I can assure him he will have my en-dorsation and vote in regard to any measures taken to accomplish that end.

I should like to inquire
of the minister whether anything has been done respecting the rural mail carriers. Of

all the employees of this department they are the worst treated in the whole of Canada and it is pretty nearly time that parliament felt ashamed of itself. This matter has been brought up time and again in the house and it is a condition that should be remedied. It is absolutely the worst instance in the whole civil service of employees being underpaid.

Is the hon. gentleman
speaking of rural mail carriers?
That is what I am talking about.

I am in favour of higher remuneration for the mail carriers, and I have several times advocated the introduction of legislation for that purpose. The trouble is that in some parishes there are people who are crazy enough to submit a ridiculously low tender in order to get the contract. Apparently they consider it an honour to work for nothing. They are a nuisance to the community. When the fair value of a contract would be, say, $600, one or two people-one is enough- in a parish will be foolish enough to submit a tender for half that amount. The man who gets the contract is proud of it, and afterwards he complains to the member that he is not well enough paid. That is the way it goes. I know a gentleman who has been around this house for several years, who charges each of these mail carriers $5, and in that way collects for himself a sum aggregating about $5,000 a year. His name is Garfield McKinnon. He comes around this building with his propaganda urging that the salaries of these men should be increased. If there was some wav of stopping the present stupid system of tendering under which a bid far too low is submitted and often gets the contract, there would be no trouble of that kind.
The way to stop it is to stop the tendering system altogether.

If the tendering system
were stopped, then my hon. friends opposite would complain that the minister was giving the contracts to his friends. It is a very difficult proposition. I am sorry that the situation exists, but the remedy does not depend upon the department any more than upon my hon. friends who have just spoken. The trouble is with the men in the different parishes who are silly enough to underestimate the value of the contract and submit a low bid in order to take the contract away from another fellow who is carrying it on satisfactorily at a reasonable rate. I am sure no one in this house will deny that that sort of thing is going on.

Supply-Post Office
Another thing: if these poor mail carriers were not silly enough to pay $5 a head to Garfield McKinnon, who goes around the corridors of the house with his propaganda that these men are underpaid, they would be better off. But he lives like a gentleman at their expense, and then comes here and complains that they are not getting enough money. The first point in his propaganda should be to urge all tenderers for mail contracts to put in a reasonable tender, and then there would be no trouble at all. Very often I go to the department to see Mr. Anderson, who is the friend of every member of this house, and he will tell me that such and such a tender is too low, but he says, we have to award it because that was the lowest tender. If that were not done I am sure we should soon hear from hon. gentlemen on the other side of the house. They would at once protest because the contract had not been awarded to the lowest tenderer, and would say that there was waste and no economy in the department. In other words they would preach exactly the opposite of what they are preaching now. I have great respect for my hon. friend from Lincoln, who is a business man, and if he could find a way of getting these people to submit decent tenders, I should be glad to broadcast his advice from this house with a view to getting better pay for the mail carriers. That man Garfield McKinnon is a pest to this house.

I was asked by an hon.
gentleman if I had done anything since last year in connection with the rural mail carriers. This applies not only to the mail carriers on what are called the rural routes, the mail box routes, but to all contractors carrying His Majesty's mail in the rural districts, say from office to office, and so forth, and to the mail carriers in small towns who are carrying mail from the station to the post office, and vice versa. The claim has been made that the carriers on all these routes should be put on a yearly salary basis at a rate for the longer hauls of S70 a mile, and that the shorter hauls should be rated in a different way. I have had the officials of the dapartment go very fully into the matter, and I find that to grant what was asked would mean an extra cost of S7,000.000 a year for the transportation of mails by land alone in Canada. The Post Office department, at the present time at least cannot stand that increased expenditure.
I recognize that in some respects the tender system is a bad one because in numerous cases the tenderers have no idea of what it will cost them to carry on the work efficiently. Only within the last day or two I have had several applications for increases in mail con-2419- noi
tracts from individuals who tendered a year or so ago and got the contract because they put in the lowest tender, and now they find that they cannot do it for the money. The only remedy I have under the existing postal service law is to say to these people, " If you find you cannot do the work for the amount for which you tendered and upon which you received the contract, we will grant you the privilege of retiring from the contract and call for new tenders." But even when we make that offer, they will not accept it.
May I say further to the committee that out of a large number of offers of renewals of existing contracts that we have made, only four per cent of these renewals at the former price have been refused. Under these circumstances I cannot see how anybody can reasonably accuse the Post Office department of not treating these mail carriers right.
What the hon. member for Temiscouata has said is true to a certain extent. Up to three or four years ago there was no movement in Canada for placing these mail carriers on a salary basis. The individual that he named is the self-constituted secretary of an unorganized so-called postal carriers' association. I do not know how far this individual travels to the west, but I know that he has travelled right down to the Atlantic coast and has been in my own county. He goes to each mail carrier, whether he has a rural route or a post office route, and obtains from each $5, in some cases $2, and in other cases what he can get, as secretary of this so-called organization. I know whereof I speak because I have the evidence. He tells them that he is about to obtain for them an increase in the amount of their mail contracts.
What objection is there to that?

Because it is not an organized association of mail carriers. The postal department recognizes every organization within the postal service that is properly organized, but not a self constituted organization of two men only.
He is representing these men, is he not?
No, he is not even a mail carrier himself.
He is paid by the men.

No, he goes around and collects money under false pretences for work he says he is doing, but is not doing.
Supply-Post Office
But, Mr. Chairman, what does it matter if the cause is good?
Up to that date there was no complaint as to the tender system.
As the minister well knows, this American system has been urged in this house for the last ten years.
It could not have been, because it has not been in vogue in the United States until the last six or seven years.

I am not suggesting the figure of seventy dollars a mile; I am referring to the system. When the minister says it has been in vogue only for the last three years, I wish to say that I spoke in this house on the question at some considerable length long before that period.
We do not want to copy anything from the States.
That is running true to form.

The American postal department are very sorry to-day that they ever adopted that system, and they would be glad to get clear of it. They find it is not working out satisfactorily. Now, when it means an additional expenditure of some seven million dollars, I think the postal department is doing right in hesitating before recommending to this house the change in the contract system.
Mr. Chairman, all that the Postmaster General has said sounds very much like a rehash of what he gave us last session.
It is the same thing, it is true.
The matter is in just the same position as it was last year.
It is.

I have before me what he said to the house last session, and there is no intimation from him that he has done anything in the meantime. Let me correct the minister. I am not aware that any member of this house suggested seventy dollars a mile as a minimum rate for rural mail carriers at all.

I did not say any hon.
member had done so.
Mr. STEW7ART (Leeds): But it is upon the seventy dollar a mile rate that the Postmaster General raises this enormous figure of seven million dollars. There were several [Mr. Veniot.l
other suggestions made to him, one of them I recall being about as follows: that a study should be made of these different routes, that they should be classified under, say, four or five classifications-they are not all alike, the conditions vary-and for class one the rate should be perhaps only forty dollars a mile-
The average rate throughout Canada now is over forty-five dollars a mile.

That may be so; some may be very high and others low. I am suggesting that only as an illustration. The second might be forty-five or fifty dollars or higher. That suggestion was made to the minister. I have before me Hansard of 1929, and I find at page 1631 the minister was dealing with this question. Let me quote:
Mr. Veniot:	If the hon. member desires me
to do so, I will have the contracts gone over and I will produce the information this week.
I do not intend to deal with this matter at any greater length, beyond repeating what I said at the beginning. My attention was called to it in a casual way in 1928, and later on my attention was more closely drawn to it, I think towards the end of 1928. But from the spring of 1928 to the present time, some attention has been paid to the existing system, and we are reviewing the situation to see whether or not a more equitable system can be put into practice.
Mr. Bennett: I think the hon. member means 1927, because he will remember that in 1928 we discused the matter.
Mr. Veniot:	Yes, it was in 1927 that my
attention was first drawn to it. I thank the hon. member for the correction. I feel that I have enough information now to warrant my saying that the application of the United States system in Canada is an impossibility. But I do not say that a better system than the one we have cannot be put into practice and it is with that end in view we are at present reviewing the situation.
Apparently the situation has been under review and there is no remedy suggested; instead, an attack has been made on a gentleman who has, I submit, a perfect right to do what he is doing in the interests of these rural mail carriers. What possible objection can there be to a man, satisfactory to this class of public servants, going around interviewing them, getting first-hand knowledge of conditions and looking after their interests, and receiving from them, voluntarily, such contributions as they wish to make to him, he in turn presenting their claims to the Postmaster General for relief and help? I cannot see any objection to that. The Postmaster General seems to think his activities are beyond the pale altogether and says this man is extorting money from the people. On what does he base any such statement?

Supply-Post Office

I will answer my hon.
friend right now. I have letters received from mail carriers throughout the country asking who this man is and what right he has to demand money from them.
He has no right.

That is not
extortion; they are not compelled to pay him anything unless they wish to do so. It is a purely voluntary arrangement.
They say not.

The minister is
endeavouring to hide behind a smoke-screen; he is not dealing with this question honestly or fairly, nor is he treating this class of public servants as they should be treated. From year to year there is the same evasion; the matter is under consideration, we are reviewing it. But he does not get anywhere with it, and I do not think he intends to do so.

Mr. Chairman, I have expressed myself on two or three occasions in the past on this matter and I have very little to say now. I have no charge to make against the minister in this connection, but I want to say to him in all sincerity that I do not think there is a servant in the service of Canada as poorly paid as the rural mail carrier. Taking the average route, which is perhaps fifteen miles, the average pay is about forty-five dollars a mile-$675-for working every day in the year except one day, unless there has been some change made since two or three years ago when, I understand, one holiday a year was granted. I am not including Sundays, of course.
The hon. gentleman is mistaken; they are not all daily services.
As far as my county is concerned they are daily services. There may be an isolated case or two.
It is not an isolated case at all; there are hundreds of them.

I am speaking of the settled
parts of the country. Take my own county of Simcoe-I presume it is typical and therefore take it as an illustration. As far as I know every solitary rural service in the county of Simcoe is a daily service, excluding Sundays. Will the minister say that is not so?
That is the rural service?
That is all I am speaking of.
We are talking generally now of mail carriers. The hon. gentleman will excuse me, but I just wish to put the record right.
There need not be any misunderstanding.

You have in your locality
regular services three times a week.

I am speaking of the rural
mail carriers; I thought the minister would know that when I took a typical route of fifteen miles at $45 a mile. Is there any other postal service that that would apply to except the rural mail carrier?

Certainly, there is the
service from post office to post office, which is not a rural box service.
That is not by the mile, though.

Yes it is, and it is under
tender the same as the others.

That is quite immaterial, anyway. I wish to make my statement very definite and I would like the minister to understand it. I am directing my remarks towards the conditions affecting the rural mail carriers. Let us take the case of the average service of fifteen miles for every day in the week except Sundays at an average cost of $45; some are as low as $40 and some as high as $60, but we will take the average of $45 a mile, which makes a total of $675. That is not $2 a day all the year round, and as far as I know these men have only one holiday in the year with the exception of Sundays. They have to maintain a motor car for summer service and one or two horses for winter. I have nothing to say against the civil servants; I have nothing to say against mail carriers from the cities, but when I hear of pleas being made on behalf of the urban carries for increased pay I wonder what those who are seeking assistance for them think of the salaries paid to rural carriers. No matter what the weather may be or what the condition of the roads, the rural mail carrier has to cover his route. In many places the roads are in wretched conditions; while the carrier can remain on the main highway his progress is somewhat easier, but when he turns to the side lines and concessions in many cases he cannot get throught without extreme difficulty. The only answer is that the work is let by tender and the department takes the attitude that it will not pay more if it can get it done for the small sum which is paid to the rural carrier. I say to the minister that there is not a service of the government let out by tender which could not be performed for less money than is paid at the present time. I hold no brief for Mr. McKinnon; in some respects I think they could get a better advocate, but I am not here to
Supply-Post Office

say anything about him. The fact that these men, voluntarily or with a little persuasion see fit to, have Mr. McKinnon represent them is a matter of their own concern. It does not belong to me and it does not belong to the minister; if they choose to let Mr. McKinnon represent them it is entirely their own affair. I am not advocating the payment of $70 a mile; I do not think it is fair to take that attitude, but in my opinion it is a matter which should be worked out. In the main, there are two kinds of routes; there are the routes where the roads are sandy or hilly and where travel is difficult, and there are the routes where the roads are good and the country is more or less level. It might be that one price should be fixed for certain routes and another price for others. It is my view that steps should be taken towards fixing, not a living wage but something within the realm of fairness for the services of these rural carriers.

They do not do this work
for a living.

I have heard that statement
before. We are told that very early in the morning when the dew is on the ground they could go out and hoe potatoes and that when they come in at night they could do something else. The point is, however, that these men have to be on the job. They have to plug through in the winter with the horses and use the motor in the summer, true, they might use the motor for other purposes. I am sure the minister will not say to this house that he thinks $675 is sufficient remuneration for a rural mail carrier who covers a route of fifteen miles. Surely the minister will not say that;-I know he is too fair-minded to suggest such a thing. No doubt his answer will be that the department calls for tenders and that if the carriers are content to work for such small salaries they may do so.

The tenderer does not
think he is worth a greater sum when he puts in his tender.

Oh, yes he does; not one of
them is satisfied. Many of these men have been devoting themselves to the service for some years; they have horses and motors, and if they lost the work they would not have anything to do. In many cases they are men sixty or sixty-five years old and as their powers of labour are becoming limited they do not want to give up the work. This work provides a living for them. I believe the time has come, in view of increases in

other lines of work, when the minister should consider some increases for the rural mail carriers. I made the statement that I had addressed remarks to this particular question on another occasion, and to substantiate my statement I have before me Hansard of April 13, 1923. On that occasion and on several others I made some statements upon this subject. The minister may rest assured that this suggestion of a given rate per mile has not been developed in the last two or three years. I endorse what has been said on behalf of the rural mail carriers; I do not wish to see them get an extraordinary amount and I would not suggest that the country could afford to pay an increased expenditure of $7,000,000. However there is a big difference between that total and an increase from the present rate to $55 or $60. I do not believe such an increase would any more than exhaust the surplus about which the minister boasts at the present time.
I am boasting of no surplus, because there is none.

I thought there was a surplus
of $2,000,000.

I wish to revert to
the question of letter carriers. For the last four years, with one exception, I have mentioned the high cost of living in the border cities. In 1927 the minister promised me that he would look i-nto the situation and in 1928 he replied as follows:
Mr. Veniot:	I did look into it and I made
a recommendation to the Civil Service Commission for an increase in salary. That recommendation has not been acted upon and I am not in a position to do any more.
I would like to know what increase that recommendation was for and whether it was to cover the extra cost of living.
If I remember correctly the documents were laid on the table last year.
I was not here at that time last year.

If I remember correctly
the recommendation was for an increase in the minimum and the maximum so that the employees would, receive over $100 a month to begin with.

I was under the impression that it was $60 a year or $5 a month. If I am correctly informed, the responsibility of the letter carriers in the cities has considerably increased during the last four or five years. Apparently there are many more

Supply-Post Office
circulars and parcels to be delivered; there is the sale of stamps, and numerous other duties have to be attended, to. In 1920 the letter carriers of Canada were receiving more than the letter carriers in the city of Detroit. I agree with the sentiments expressed by the hon. member for North Simcoe. In Grey county I think in all cases we have daily mail service, and that is a county hard to travel, with a number of hilly back roads. I believe the rural mail carriers in Southeast Grey are very badly paid,
and while I realize that under the tender system it is their own fault, yet there are just two kinds of people who submit these tenders. On the one hand you have the man who has been doing the work, who has the equipment, and who fears that he will be underbid by an inexperienced man who may not know the cost of the equipment or the work which will be required. The inexperienced man is likely to tender at a lower figure than the man who has the equipment, and the other man feels that to hold his job he must put in a still lower bid, with the result that the man who gets the contract does the work for less than it is worth.
The minister says the government cannot afford to pay the carriers any more. I would respectfully suggest that it would have been better to keep the postage rate at three cents and pay the men who deliver our mail a living wage than to reduce the postage to two cents

and not pay a fair wage. I realize that it will not be an easy thing to change the whole method of paying rural mail carriers, but surely some system could be introduced better than the one we have now. I know there are probably half a dozen different kinds of routes, but surely they could be graded and wages paid according to the kind of route covered. In communities where they can use a car all year round, with improved highways on which to travel, it may be a simple matter to deliver the mail in a very short time with an old car, but in the county of Grey these carriers cannot possibly use a car in the winter time and unfortunately we only have about six months of summer. Then it becomes very hard work for these rural mail carriers to make their rounds. I do not know of any service that has brought as much joy and contentment to those living in the country as has been brought by the rural mail delivery. Had I been choosing a secretary for the rural mail carriers I am quite frank to say my choice might have been different, but that is nothing to me and I doubt if it is anything to the Postmaster General. I am quite sure that if the rural mail carriers had not felt that they were poorly paid and had a real grievance no one on earth would have been able to secure money from them to improve conditions. I want to say these few words to help the other members who are seeking to have something done to better the condition of the rural mail carriers.

When I made my few remarks a short time ago I did not have Hansard before me. Well, it must work out fairly in the United States or they would not have adopted it there.

Since I have been in this house this question has come up every year, and I think it hardly worth while to try to convince the minister that he should do something for these people who are so poorly paid. However, there is one question I should like to bring to his attention. I should like to know if there is a fair wage clause inserted in the contracts for mail collection in the big cities?
Yes.

The sum is not fixed, but it is supposed to be the wages paid for similar work in the city where the contract is let.

I may say that I have had only one complaint along this line, which came about three or four weeks ago from Vancouver, if I am not mistaken, and the departmental officials immediately took up the matter with the contractor. The complaint was that the contractor was paying very small wages to those who collected the mail from the boxes. We took up the matter at once and are awaiting a report from our superintendent.

The information I have comes from the city of Toronto. It is true that the revenue is not large, and prehaps that is a reason why the postmaster has not been paid more, but this community is now without a post office because remuneration is so small and no one can be found to take the office at $181 a year. If all they can say is: "If we raise the mail carriers to a minimum of $1,200 we shall have to raise other civil servants to a similar minimum , then I think the Postmaster General, together with his colleagues should say, "'Very well, that is perfectly satisfactory to us, because we do not want to see any of our adult male workers at a salary less than twenty-five dollars a week of $100 a month". Let me remind the hon. minister that in 1924 the then Postmaster General recommended that the maximum salary of these men be $1,560. They were then getting a cost of living bonus. The cost

of living has not decreased since 1924. But in answer to that recommendation of the then Postmaster General the Civil Service Commission did what? The third involves a consideration of the entire sources of revenue- stamps, money orders, and the carriage of newspapers and parcels. One other matter. We have said that we think no civil servant should have less than $100 a month. I should like to think that everybody must be agreed about that, that twenty-five dollars a week, roughly speaking -it is not quite that as a matter of fact- is not too much. Is not this the difficulty, that we are creating too many civil servants, with the result that we are not paying some of them a decent wage? I should like to say that we who sit to the left of the Speaker will support the government in any measure they may introduce looking towards reasonable compensations being paid to the civil servants of this country, and nothing less than $100 a month is a reasonable salary upon which a man can live, and certainly live and support a family.

If the Civil Service Commission is standing in the way of this parliament I should be very much surprised. With the permission of the committee I should like to speak to the previous item dealing with public buildings in New Brunswick, since I was not here when this item was called. I desire to direct attention to the fact that throughout the entire province of New Brunswick provision is made for only one new public building this year, at Atholville in the county of Restigouche. It should be of interest to the committee to know that Atholville, or Athol as it is commonly called, is a small village situated two miles west of Campbellton in the county of Restigouche. Recently a large pulp mill was erected there, but the offices of the company are in the town of Campbellton, and I should say that the revenue from that post office at Athol could not exceed $1,000 a year. I am just estimating that amount, but I know that all the business of the corporations which operate in the west end of Campbellton and in Athol is done in Campbellton, where they have their executive offices.
In the distribution of public money and in the erection of public buildings surely some principle should prevail other than the wish of the sitting member. There is no public service conducted at Atholville except the post office; there is no customs house or anything of that kind, and I do submit that there are many places in the province of New Brunswick which are entitled to public buildings before a small community like Athol is considered. For five years or more I have been asking the minister for a post office in the town of McAdam, where there is a public revenue of between $40,000 and $50,000 per year. another furniture item; Krug Furniture Company, Kitchener, 33 chairs, $1,107.70 -very expensive chairs, I would think; renewing wooden terrace platform, installing surface drain and grading grounds, $4,566.80; interior decorating, $3,218.10; sundry painting and repairs, $1,907.87; electrical supplies, $164.80; locks, door sets, et cetera, $86154; plumbing supplies, $523.09; carpets-another item-Morgan and Company, Montreal, $388.89; dishes, $1,320.73; electrical fixtures, $3,330.80; furniture, $1,332; linoleum, $1,034.80, and many other items. Then I find also this further expenditure: pictures, $204.92; radio, $545; window shades, $307.63; sundries, $2,367.85; cleaning, painting, etc., $328.05; kitchen equipment, $1,91857. Then there is still another furniture item of $1,070. It seems to me, Mr. Chairman, that something ought to be done to curtail that kind of expenditure. Is any check kept on this furniture?

It is not the intention to establish vice-regal quarters in other sections of the Dominion. We are simply continuing the quarters that for years past have been maintained for His Majesty's representative in Canada.
For how many years?
Since 1871.
I have the figures back for twenty years and the annual expenditure has been about $2,000.

That is correct. In 1927 there was a general desire that those old, historic and very beautiful quarters in the city of Quebec, on a site unequalled I think on the North American continent, should not be allowed to fall further into disrepair.
But 'these are new buildings.
No, this is a reconstruction of the former buildings with some additions in order that this old historic citadel should not be allowed to fall into decay.
Was all this furniture and equipment necessary to preserve the building?

No, but there would not
be much object in preserving, restoring and reconstructing a building if furniture were not placed in it. I have given my hon. friend details of the costs of reconstruction and furnishing. When my hon. friend considers the matter, and especially if he will give himself the pleasure and satisfaction of going down there and visiting this place-

Is this an invitation to go down?
Yes, certainly it is.
May I remind the minister that I would not be permitted to go into the building if I did go down there?

Oh yes, you would be
permitted.

A friend of mine visited there some time ago and on my advice he went to see the citadel. I told him that it was a place of historic interest, and on his return he told me he was not allowed to go in.

I would like to know the
name of the gentleman who was refused admission and if possible the name of the gentleman who refused him admission. I have no doubt that my hon. friend, with his appearance, would be admitted if he cared to make application.
I might tell my hon. friend that I was through the citadel a few weeks ago.

Oh, but you are the chief
whip.

Seriously, I wish to say to the committee that in my opinion it was in the interests of the country that for the maintenance of historic traditions these expenditures should have been made. There has been an excellent result. I believe that the contact with the sister province of Quebec in reviving the old custom of having His Majesty's representative reside there a portion of each year has had very beneficial results. The representative is enabled to become better acquainted with the different portions of the country and particularly with the picturesque sections. To my mind that is something highly desirable and in the interests of the whole of Canada. I am satisfied that anybody who looks at the building will be delighted. The citizens of this country have the opportunity of visiting it and I regret the fact that any citizen has been refused admission. I think the application must not have been made in the manner in which my hon. friend would have made it. We have received value for the money expended, and I believe the result has more than justified the decision of the committee that the citadel should be restored. The original cost was great, and the building is of great value to Canada. I would particularly request members of this committee to visit the citadel when they have occasion to be in the city of Quebec, and in that way they may gather an idea of the value of this building.

The minister has spoken
seriously in regard to this matter. I think gentlemen on this side of the house are as much concerned as he is with the dignity of government. I want to tell the hon. gentleman that there is a growing conviction in this country that under his regime vice-royalty has been a very expensive proposition, and I think the committee should know how much viceroyalty has cost the country in the last few years. I venture to say the sum will astonish the taxpayers of this country. The money expended on Rideau hall, the citadel at Quebec, new private cars and the refurnishing of everything used by vice-royalty would astonish the taxpayers.
I think the taxpayers have been kept pretty well informed from time to time.

I would like to have the
full information in regard to this matter; I would like to know how much it has cost in the last three years, and I ask the minister to get that information.

I shall be pleased to give
our expenditures.

I am satisfied the amount will run into hundreds of thousands of dollars and will be very much more than it has been in previous years. We have had governors general going to Quebec year in and year out, but we have never had suggested anything like the expenditure on the citadel proposed by the present Minister of Public Works. I daresay his remarks were true when he told of the condition into which the citadel had fallen, but I think the sum required for reconstruction is extremely large, and he will have to justify the expenditure to this house and to the country. To my mind this would be a good place to close discussion so that the minister may have an opportunity to get the information. We want to have full details of the total expenditures for Rideau hall, for the citadel and for travelling accommodation for the governor general.
I assume the hon. member does not require repetition of the information I have just given.
No, not as to the citadel.

I shall be pleased to furnish the hon. member with any information I have as to the items he has mentioned. I would like to ask him how far back he wishes to go, because if he will compare the repairs and expenditures of recent years with those of past years he will find that in comparison the recent expenditures have been very moderate.

To what years does the
minister refer?

I would say about 1914
and 1915.

How much was spent at
that time?

Over $200,000 was spent
on Rideau hall.

We are speaking of the
citadel at the present time.
My hon. friend has referred to both the citadel and Rideau hall.

As far as I am concerned
the minister can go back as far as he likes; the farther back he goes, the better. What method is adopted in making these purchases? Are the purchases made through a government purchasing agent, or otherwise?

They are made through
a purchasing agent.
